title: ADR-000: Common evaluation criteria for all tool selections
description:
Define the shared evaluation template that every ADR (001–010) will apply. Produces a reusable criteria rubric and a short prose section that each ADR includes by reference.

## Why this exists

Each ADR will evaluate different tools against different functional requirements, but a set of cross-cutting criteria applies to all of them. Defining these once avoids drift between ADRs and forces each decision to be honest about the same hard constraints.

## Budget constraint

**Budget is effectively 0€.** This is a first-class filter, not a soft preference. It means:
- Managed cloud services (Confluent Cloud, Datadog, Temporal Cloud, AWS MSK, etc.) are disqualified unless they have a genuinely usable free tier with no credit-card-required production cliff.
- Self-hosted open-source is the default mode.
- Tools with open-core models are acceptable only if the features required by the architecture sit in the free/community tier — the ADR must explicitly verify this.
- Licensing traps (BSL, SSPLv1, ELv2, Commons Clause) must be flagged even if currently free, because they constrain future use.

## Criteria to define

1. **Cost / licensing** — total cost of self-hosting (infra, ops time) vs free tier limits; licence type and change risk.
2. **Regulatory fit** — GDPR (data residency, right to erasure), DORA (resilience testing, RTO/RPO documentation), PSD2 (audit trail, SCA). Hard pass/fail before functional comparison.
3. **Operational complexity at small scale** — how much ops burden does this add to a small team? Preference for tools that degrade gracefully when not actively tuned.
4. **Ecosystem coherence** — does it compose with the rest of the chosen stack without bespoke glue? Native OpenTelemetry, standard connectors, etc.
5. **Exit cost** — how painful is migration away in 3–5 years? Does the tool own a data format or protocol that creates lock-in?
6. **Community and longevity** — is this tool likely to still be maintained in 10 years? Red flags: single-vendor control with recent licence change, stagnant commits, small contributor base.
7. **Functional fit** — tool-specific criteria defined per ADR.

## Deliverable

A markdown section titled '## Common Evaluation Criteria' usable as a template block in each ADR, plus a summary rubric table (criteria × weight) that each ADR fills in for its candidates.
acceptance_criteria: Template section written and agreed. Each ADR-001–010 issue updated to reference this template.

title: product_concepts/04-open-questions.md: surface the deferred decisions
description:
Write the open-questions doc — the place where genuinely deferred decisions live, with enough context that a future session knows what would unblock each.

Required questions (each gets a context paragraph + an 'unblocked by' note):

1. Competitive positioning — Temenos T24, Mambu, Thought Machine Vault, 10x, Tuum, Finxact. What's the credible PT-incumbent wedge vs each? (Unblocked by competitive landscape research.)

2. Pricing model — per-account / per-product-line / platform fee / hybrid. Affects sales motion and unit economics. (Unblocked by customer-development interviews.)

3. Licensing posture — closed-source vendor / commercial-open-source / open-source-with-managed-service. Affects GTM heavily, including how easy it is for incumbents to evaluate. (Unblocked by founder/team strategic decision.)

4. Legacy coexistence targets — which PT cores need first-class coexistence stories (BANKA, AS400-era, internal stacks). (Unblocked by market research on PT core banking landscape.)

5. SaaS multi-tenancy isolation level — shared DB with row-level tenancy / DB-per-tenant / cluster-per-tenant. Big regulator and ops implication. (Unblocked by a security/compliance review of typical PT bank requirements.)

6. IFRS 9 signal boundary — what signals the subledger emits to feed external IFRS 9 systems (staging triggers, days-past-due, restructuring events). Out of scope to implement IFRS 9, but in scope to define the signal contract. (Unblocked by an IFRS 9 SME conversation.)

7. Time-travel / point-in-time correctness — required for audit, dispute resolution. Event-sourcing vs snapshot-and-journal. (Unblocked by a target-customer audit-requirements discussion.)

8. Configurability depth — template catalog only / DSL only / both (templates for 80%, DSL for the long tail). Heart of the 'agility' wedge. (Unblocked by prototyping the configuration surface.)

title: product_concepts/02-v1-scope-term-deposits.md: write the v1 concrete slice
description:
Write the document that makes the brief concrete — the v1 product slice. Term deposits chosen because they exercise the engine + PT regulatory pack at minimum surface, and align perfectly with the integration_concepts/ running example.

Required content:

Why term deposits as v1 — simplest CF math (§5), narrowest PT regulatory surface, aligns with integration_concepts/ running example. Validates the engine end-to-end before adding complexity.

In-scope features — depósito a prazo with the three interest-payment variants from financial_concepts §5.3:
- Interest at maturity (most common)
- Periodic interest (monthly/quarterly)
- Interest paid in advance (juros antecipados)

PT regulatory features in v1:
- TANB/TANL split with 28% IRS withholding tax on interest
- Act/360 day-count convention
- TAE per §5.4 (effective annual rate with compounding)
- Banco de Portugal reporting hooks (signals emitted; reports themselves are downstream)

Subledger outputs — deposit position, accrual schedule, maturity calendar, withholding ledger.

Event contract — the API the rest of the bank's systems consume. Name events per the conventions in integration_concepts/08-event-catalog-governance.md. Suggested set: DepositConstituted, InterestAccrued, WithholdingApplied, DepositMatured, DepositRenewed, DepositTerminatedEarly.

Coexistence with legacy DDA — term deposits settle into a current account, which lives in the bank's legacy core. Document the coexistence APIs that make this work without double-counting.

Explicit out-of-scope for v1 — structured deposits, FX deposits, secondary-market trading, deposit-guarantee-fund reporting, early-withdrawal penalty schedules beyond the simplest case.

title: product_concepts/01-product-architecture.md: write the architectural thesis
description:
Write the heart of the brief — the architectural thesis. Five sections, each one a load-bearing piece of the product's identity.

Section 1 — The cash-flow primitive. Cite and quote financial_concepts §9.2 unification equation S(t+Δt) = S(t)·(1 + r·Δt) − payments + drawdowns. Show how every banking product family collapses to this single equation. Frame it as the architectural insight that makes 'one engine across product families' possible.

Section 2 — The configuration surface. The three variable dimensions from §2.2 (cash-flow shape, day-count convention, compounding frequency) plus charges, insurance, regulatory pack. New products = configuration, not new modules. Note that this is where the 'agility' wedge lives concretely.

Section 3 — The two families inside one engine. With-a-plan (forecast cash flows; deposits, credits) vs irregular (observed cash flows; current accounts, cards). Same primitive, two operating modes — reference §8 and §9.

Section 4 — The regulatory pack. PT pack (DL 133/2009, DL 74-A/2017, BdP conventions, IRS 28% withholding, Act/360); ES pack TBD; EU baseline from CCD 2008/48/EC + MCD 2014/17/EU. Packs are swappable from day one — non-negotiable for the geographic roadmap. If regulation is buried in the engine, EU expansion costs a rewrite.

Section 5 — The integration seam. Engine inherits the architecture documented in integration_concepts/, NOT redefines it: events on Redpanda (ADR-001), schema format (ADR-002), saga participation (ADR-003), outbox emission (ADR-004), observability via OpenTelemetry (ADR-007), MCP server exposure path (ADR-010). Plus the deployment-modes story (SaaS multi-tenant + self-hosted, single codebase) and the strangler-fig coexistence patterns (per-product-line onboarding; APIs to coexist with legacy system of record; event contract that lets legacy and new engine react to each other).
acceptance_criteria: 01-product-architecture.md exists with the five sections above. Each section cross-links correctly: financial_concepts §9.2 and §2.2 for sections 1-2; integration_concepts/00, 02, 04, 05, 08 and ADRs 001/002/003/004/007/010 for section 5. The doc clearly inherits — does not redefine — the integration architecture.

title: Conceptual doc: chat agent channel strategy — inbound and outbound
description: The system's UI strategy is shifting away from traditional web/mobile frontends toward chat agents (WhatsApp, Slack, or custom LLM-powered agents). This changes the architecture in two directions: (1) Outbound — saga completion and status updates must be delivered as chat messages (via WhatsApp Business API, Slack webhooks, or similar), not SSE streams. This is the async notification problem (tracked separately), but the chat-platform specifics (message formatting, conversation thread continuity, handling multi-step approvals via chat reply) need their own treatment. (2) Inbound — messages arriving from chat platforms are HTTP POST webhooks sent to the bank's edge by the platform (WhatsApp cloud API, Slack Events API). The gateway must route these inbound webhooks to a chat adapter service that interprets natural-language or structured messages as banking commands (constitute deposit, check balance, confirm approval). The chat adapter is itself a bounded context and likely needs an ACL to translate platform-native message formats into domain commands. Decisions needed: which chat platform(s) to support; whether a single adapter handles all platforms or each platform has its own adapter; how conversational context (multi-turn saga flows) is maintained across platform messages; how human approval steps in the saga surface as interactive chat messages (approval buttons, reply-based confirmation). Deliverable: a new conceptual document in integration_concepts/ covering the chat agent channel pattern, its integration points with the existing saga/event backbone, and the trust model for inbound platform webhooks.
notes: Resolved as the bank-as-MCP-server pattern (third-party LLM agent, untrusted caller), not the platform-webhook pattern the original description framed (WhatsApp/Slack). WhatsApp/Slack acknowledged in doc 11 only as user-side surfaces in front of the agent, not as the bank's integration concern. title: ADR-011: Async saga completion notification — out-of-band callback wire format
description: The SSE stream_url pattern in ADR-006 and doc 05 assumes an actively waiting client (browser, mobile app). For sagas with workflow-approval steps that take hours or days, SSE is structurally wrong: the connection dies when the client moves on. Chat agents and async clients need a callback/webhook model instead: the initiating request includes a callback_url, and the orchestrator (or a dedicated notification service) posts the terminal outcome to that URL when the saga completes. Decisions needed: (1) callback URL registration — field on the request body vs. a separate subscription endpoint; (2) delivery guarantees — at-least-once with idempotency key on the callback payload; (3) HMAC signature on outbound webhooks so the receiver can verify authenticity; (4) retry policy for failed deliveries (transient network errors, recipient downtime); (5) which component owns delivery — orchestrator directly, or a dedicated notification service that subscribes to saga terminal events from the backbone; (6) whether the existing SSE path and the webhook path coexist (bifurcated by presence of callback_url in the request) or whether SSE is deprecated in favour of webhooks for all clients. Deliverable: decision captured in either a new ADR or as an amendment to ADR-006 and doc 00/05.
close_reason: ADR-011 written: pre-registered subscription endpoint (SSRF mitigation), at-least-once with HMAC-SHA256 + timestamp, exponential backoff 10 attempts over 12h, dedicated notification service as choreography consumer, SSE and callbacks coexist. Four implementation principles: subscription lifecycle, delivery envelope, notification service as choreography consumer, 202 response amendment.

title: Revisit ADR-011 D6: evaluate fully deprecating the saga status SSE stream for all clients
description:
ADR-011 D6 decided that SSE (the stream_url in the 202 response, doc 05 / ADR-006) coexists with webhook callbacks rather than being deprecated. The rationale was that SSE remains correct for browser/mobile clients that can hold a connection.

The question to re-examine: should the saga status SSE be deprecated for ALL clients — including browser/mobile — in favour of polling (get_process_status, Pattern 2) + callbacks (Pattern 3, ADR-011)?

Background:
- The MCP transport SSE (HTTP+SSE from spec 2024-11-05) is already deprecated and replaced by Streamable HTTP per ADR-010. That is a separate and settled matter.
- The saga status SSE is NOT Streamable HTTP's replacement target. Streamable HTTP is MCP-specific; browsers don't use MCP. If the saga status SSE were deprecated, the replacement for browser clients would be polling + callbacks, not Streamable HTTP.
- Keeping SSE means Kong must maintain the extended read_timeout and X-Accel-Buffering:no configuration (ADR-006 P4) indefinitely. It also means the 202 response carries stream_url for all clients even if most will ignore it once the webhook path matures.

Arguments for deprecating:
- One completion model (polling + callbacks) for all clients simplifies the surface considerably: one path to maintain, test, and document
- Browser/mobile clients can use polling (get_process_status) for saga tracking; the UX is slightly less real-time but adequate for sagas that take hundreds of milliseconds to complete
- The SSE path is the operationally complex one (long-lived connections, Kong read_timeout tuning, load balancer idle timeout configuration)

Arguments against deprecating:
- Browser UX for fast sagas (~700ms) regresses: instead of watching the saga complete in near-real-time, the client must poll
- Owned clients (bank's own mobile app, web frontend) should not be forced to adopt an async model that was designed for disconnected agents
- ADR-011 D6 was a deliberate decision with a sound rationale; revisiting it should require a concrete trigger

Deliverable: either affirm ADR-011 D6 (coexistence is correct) with a note on when to revisit, or produce an amendment to ADR-006, ADR-011, and docs 00/05 that removes stream_url and the SSE path.
close_reason:
Evaluated — affirm ADR-011 D6: coexistence is correct.

Rationale:
1. The 202 arrives in ~150ms; the saga finishes in ~850ms. For a browser client watching 'Processing...', SSE delivers real-time completion with zero polling latency. Replacing SSE with polling adds 0-500ms perceived latency and extra round-trips — a real regression for owned browser/mobile clients.

2. The operational concern (long-lived connections, Kong config) is already closed: ADR-006 P4 documents exactly the required Kong configuration (extended read_timeout, X-Accel-Buffering:no). Operational surface is a few lines of kong.yaml, not ongoing burden.

3. No concrete trigger exists. The issue's own text says 'revisiting should require a concrete trigger.'

Trigger conditions for future revisitation:
- If the bank's owned browser/mobile clients are redesigned to go through MCP (at which point MCP tasks + get_process_status already exist and SSE becomes genuinely redundant)
- If Kong SSE proxying produces measurable operational incidents in a production environment
- If the polling + callback path proves sufficient in a production deployment and the SSE path adds no meaningful UX benefit over polling with aggressive intervals (<200ms)

title: ADR-010 candidate: MCP server runtime and SDK selection
description: Doc 11 (chat agent channel strategy, archie-407) commits to exposing a bank-owned MCP server as the integration surface for LLM agents but does not pick the runtime, SDK, or transport implementation. Candidates include the official Python SDK (modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk), TypeScript SDK (modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk), or a Go/Rust implementation; transport choice between Streamable HTTP (current default for remote servers in MCP spec 2025-11-25) and SSE; hosting model (alongside the existing edge gateway behind Kong from ADR-006, or as a separate service with its own ingress); and the OAuth 2.1 authorisation server integration (existing IAM that already issues JWTs for the REST edge, vs. a dedicated MCP-specific authorisation server with dynamic client registration enabled). This ADR should follow the ADR-000 evaluation framework and reference doc 11 as the conceptual grounding for what the MCP server must support (tools, resources, prompts, elicitation form+url modes, tasks capability per SEP-1686, server-initiated notifications).
close_reason: ADR-010 written: Python SDK + Streamable HTTP + behind Kong + reuse existing IAM with RFC 8707/9728 extensions. Updated doc 11 'How This Connects' table to cross-link ADR-010.

title: Cross-cutting editorial sweep across ADR series
description: Apply consistent edits across all ADRs as a single pass: (1) Audit and strike 'trivially/trivial' usages — if it is trivial, the word is unnecessary; if it is not, the word is wrong. (2) Replace softener phrases ('effectively zero', 'effectively open') with the actual constraint. (3) Audit 'may/should' inside Implementation Principles sections (ADR-003 through ADR-008); principles are normative, so prefer 'must' or declarative present tense. (4) Reduce em-dash density in opening paragraphs and dense analytical passages — three em-dashes per paragraph reads as nested asides. (5) Anchor all relative date phrases ('since 2020', 'as of 2026') to the ADR header date or a specific calendar date.
close_reason: Four targeted edits across the series: (1) ADR-004 line 134 'trivially implemented' -> 'a handful of lines' (the one remaining claim-of-trivial in the series — others matching the grep are legitimate uses of 'non-trivial' meaning 'difficult'); (2) ADR-001 line 75 'effectively zero' -> 'negligible' (the assertive form); (3) ADR-002 line 89 'effectively seamless' -> 'seamless'; (4) ADR-007 P4 'should use pseudonymous identifiers wherever possible' rewritten to 'must default to pseudonymous identifiers; raw identifiers require an explicit justification at the call site that survives code review' — strengthens the normative verb while preserving the legitimate exception path. Deliberately did NOT do: em-dash reduction (28-44 per file is mostly structural use, not nested asides — flattening it would damage the author's voice for negligible clarity gain) and broad date-anchor sweep (almost all 'as of YEAR' / 'in YEAR' references already carry a year, which is itself an anchor; the residual unanchored 'since 2020' was already fixed in P2). Most 'may/should' inside Implementation Principles are normatively-correct prohibitions ('No saga may hold...') or permissions ('Services may add...').
